content: 1. The broken red line has been removed from the age-based vaccination schedule. Vaccination for individuals with specific risk factors is now represented solely by purple bars. 2. The human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine has been added to the age-based schedule. A yellow bar indicates that the vaccine is recommended for women aged 60 years. 3. A new column has been introduced in the medical/other indications schedule to clarify the indications for hepatitis A and B vaccines. The indications chronic liver disease and recipients of clotting factor concentrates have been removed from the previous schedule's third and fifth columns, respectively, and combined into this new column. The column includes a yellow bar for hepatitis A and B vaccines, specifying that these vaccines are recommended for all individuals with these medical indications. 4. The HPV vaccine has also been added to the medical/other indications schedule. A yellow bar indicates that the vaccine is recommended for women under 26 years of age with all indications except pregnancy. 5. The Tdap vaccine has been added to the medical/other indications schedule. A hatched yellow bar indicates that Tdap is a one-time, single-dose recommendation for all indications except pregnancy. 6. The tetanus and diphtheria footnote (1) has been revised to align with ACIP recommendations for the use of Tdap. 7. A new footnote (2) has been added to reflect ACIP recommendations for HPV vaccination for all women under 26 years of age. 8. The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) footnote (3) has been revised to reflect ACIP recommendations for administering a second dose of the mumps vaccine to adults in certain age groups and with specific risk factors. 9. The varicella footnote (4) has been updated in accordance with ACIP recommendations for administering a routine second dose to all adults without evidence of immunity. The footnote has also been revised to reflect the new definition of immunity to varicella. 10. The influenza footnote (5) has been updated to reflect recent ACIP recommendations to vaccinate close contacts of children aged 0–59 months, rather than 0–23 months. 11. Sexually active women who have not been infected with any of the HPV vaccine types derive the full benefit of vaccination. Vaccination is less beneficial for women who have already been infected with one or more of the four HPV vaccine types. A complete HPV vaccine series consists of three doses. The second dose should be administered two months after the first dose, and the third dose should be administered six months after the first dose. Vaccination is not recommended during pregnancy. If a woman becomes pregnant after starting the vaccination series, the remaining doses should be delayed until after the pregnancy is completed. 12. Adults born before 1957 are generally considered immune to measles. Adults born during or after 1957 should receive at least one dose of MMR unless they have a medical contraindication, documentation of at least one dose, a history of measles confirmed by a healthcare provider, or laboratory evidence of immunity. A second dose of MMR is recommended for adults who have been recently exposed to measles, are in an outbreak setting, were previously vaccinated with killed measles vaccine, were vaccinated with an unknown type of measles vaccine during 1963–1967, are students in postsecondary educational institutions, work in healthcare facilities, or plan to travel internationally. MMR or other measles-containing vaccines should not be administered to HIV-infected individuals with severe immunosuppression. 13. Adults born before 1957 are generally considered immune to mumps. Adults born during or after 1957 should receive one dose of MMR unless they have a medical contraindication, a history of mumps confirmed by a healthcare provider, or laboratory evidence of immunity. A second dose of MMR is recommended for adults in an age group affected during a mumps outbreak, students in postsecondary educational institutions, healthcare workers, or those planning international travel. For unvaccinated healthcare workers born before 1957 without other evidence of mumps immunity, consider administering one dose routinely and strongly consider a second dose during an outbreak. 14. Administer one dose of MMR vaccine to women with an unreliable rubella vaccination history or lacking laboratory evidence of immunity. For women of childbearing age, routinely determine rubella immunity and counsel them regarding congenital rubella syndrome. Do not vaccinate women who are pregnant or might become pregnant within four weeks of receiving the vaccine. Women without evidence of immunity should receive the MMR vaccine upon completion or termination of pregnancy and before discharge from the healthcare facility. 15. All adults without evidence of immunity to varicella should receive two doses of the varicella vaccine. This includes individuals such as teachers of young children, childcare employees, residents and staff of institutional settings (including correctional institutions), college students, military personnel, adolescents and adults living in households with children, non-pregnant women of childbearing age, and international travelers. Evidence of immunity includes U.S.-born individuals before 1980 (except healthcare workers and pregnant women), a history of varicella confirmed by a healthcare provider, a history of herpes zoster confirmed by a healthcare provider, or laboratory evidence of immunity or disease confirmation. Do not vaccinate women who are pregnant or might become pregnant within four weeks of receiving the vaccine. Assess pregnant women for varicella immunity. Women without evidence of immunity should receive the first dose of the varicella vaccine upon completion or termination of pregnancy and before discharge from the healthcare facility. The second dose should be administered 4–8 weeks after the first dose. 16. Adults with anatomic or functional asplenia or terminal complement component deficiencies should receive meningococcal vaccination. Vaccination is also recommended for travelers to areas with epidemic meningococcal disease, such as the meningitis belt of sub-Saharan Africa during the dry season, particularly if prolonged contact with local populations is expected. The government of Saudi Arabia requires meningococcal vaccination for all travelers to Mecca during the annual Hajj. Meningococcal conjugate vaccine is preferred for adults under 55 years of age with these indications, although meningococcal polysaccharide vaccine (MPSV4) is an acceptable alternative. 17. Hib conjugate vaccines are licensed for children aged 6 weeks to 71 months. There is no efficacy data to support a recommendation for Hib vaccine use in older children and adults with chronic conditions associated with an increased risk for Hib disease. However, studies suggest good immunogenicity in patients with sickle cell disease, leukemia, HIV infection, or those who have undergone splenectomy. Administering the vaccine to these patients is not contraindicated. 18. The recommended adult immunization schedule indicates the age groups and medical indications for routine administration of licensed vaccines for individuals aged 19 years and older as of October 1, 2006. Licensed combination vaccines may be used when any components of the combination are indicated, provided the other components are not contraindicated. For detailed recommendations on all vaccines, including those primarily used for travelers or issued during the year, consult the manufacturers' package inserts and the complete statements from the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP). 19. Report all clinically significant post-vaccination reactions to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). Reporting forms and instructions are available online or by telephone at 800-822-7967. Information on filing a Vaccine Injury Compensation Program claim is available online or by telephone at 800-338-2382. Additional information about the vaccines in this schedule and contraindications for vaccination is available online or from the CDC-INFO Contact Center at 800-CDC-INFO (800-232-4636), available in English and Spanish, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
